title: AI Visibility for SaaS: How to Win "Best Tool for X" in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI
metaTitle: AI Visibility for SaaS: Win "Best Tool for X"
metaDescription: How SaaS companies get named in "best tool for X" answers from ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI: how shortlists form, what moves them, and a 30-day plan.
shortAnswer: SaaS companies win "best tool for X" answers by showing up in the sources AI engines retrieve for that question: comparison roundups, review profiles such as G2, and their own factual pricing, integration and comparison pages, all describing the product the same way. Crawler blocking is rarely the problem. In our study of 193 SaaS sites, only one disallowed any AI search bot. Absence from the sources is.
intro:
A buyer asks ChatGPT for the best help desk for a 30-person Shopify brand and gets three or four names. Those names are the shortlist. If yours is missing, nobody rejected you; you were never evaluated.

This page covers how that shortlist forms for [software as a service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_as_a_service) (SaaS) products, which tactics move it, how to measure it, and a 30-day plan. If you sell to long buying committees or sell services too, read [AEO for B2B](/for/b2b) next.

sections.heading: Why does SaaS have so much at stake in AI answers?
sections.body:
Software buyers already compare vendors in chat. In G2's 2026 AI search report, a survey of 1,076 B2B decision-makers, [51% said they start software research with an AI chatbot more often than Google](https://learn.g2.com/g2-2026-ai-search-insight-report), and chatbots were the most-cited influence on shortlists (54%), ahead of review sites (43%).

The same report says 69% chose a different vendor than planned after an AI chatbot's guidance, and 33% bought from a vendor they had not heard of before. G2 sells to software vendors and the figures are self-reported, so read them as direction, not measurement.

Our own records point the same way. In AEOeye's recommendation benchmark (127 audits, 892 answers; small and self-selected, not a market rate), answers named 2.9 competitors on average, and a ranked brand was named first 71.4% of the time (147 ranked mentions). Being named at all is the hard part; see [how we measure it](/blog/ai-brand-recommendation-measurement).

![Overhead view of a team analyzing graphs and charts on laptops during a meeting.](https://images.pexels.com/photos/8145328/pexels-photo-8145328.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1200)

sections.heading: How does the "best tool for X" shortlist form?
sections.body:
The engine turns the question into several searches, reads what comes back and writes a short list from what those pages agree on. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may use ["query fan-out", issuing multiple related searches across subtopics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features). ChatGPT search relies on [OAI-SearchBot](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots) and Perplexity on [PerplexityBot](https://docs.perplexity.ai/guides/bots) to surface sites.

Buyers start with commercial intent. In G2's data, 33% open with a category prompt and 31% with a competitor prompt. That second number matters: your rival's name is in the question, so you must appear where "[competitor] alternatives" is answered.

The sources are mostly not yours. A 2025 arXiv study found AI search engines show [a systematic bias toward earned media over brand-owned content](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08919), unlike Google's more balanced mix. We read the shortlist as three gates (our model, not engine documentation):

- **In the pool:** a retrieved page names you for this exact use case.
- **Ranked:** several independent sources agree, recently.
- **Framed:** third parties describe you as "best for startups" or "the cheap option".

Most SaaS products pass the gate for the broad category and fail it once the buyer adds a qualifier such as team size, integration or compliance. That is the high-intent query.

sections.heading: Is blocking AI crawlers a SaaS problem?
sections.body:
Almost never. In AEOeye's crawler access study (fetched 3 October 2026, 391 well-known sites, a convenience sample rather than the web), 1 of 193 SaaS sites disallowed any AI retrieval bot, against 27 of 38 news publishers. The [per-site data is public](/resources/ai-crawler-access-study-2026-10.csv) and the [study is presented here](/blog/ai-crawler-user-agent-directory).

| In our study | SaaS | UGC and review sites | News publishers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Block at least one AI retrieval bot | 1/193 (0.5%) | 5/20 (25%) | 27/38 (71.1%) |
| Block GPTBot (training) | 4/193 (2.1%) | 6/20 (30%) | 20/38 (52.6%) |
| Valid llms.txt file | 108/180 (60%) | 4/10 | 1/29 (3.4%) |
| Homepage Organization schema | 129/176 (73.3%) | 2/6 | 24/27 (88.9%) |
| Homepage FAQPage schema | 13/176 (7.4%) | 0/6 | 0/27 |

Three readings. First, the sources you depend on are more restrictive than you are: one in four review and community sites in our sample blocks a retrieval bot, so earning coverage there takes real work. Second, 17 of 193 SaaS homepages (8.8%) blocked or challenged our own research crawler, which robots.txt would never show. Ask your infrastructure team whether your CDN lets OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot reach pricing and docs pages; both vendors [publish IP ranges](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots) for allowlisting.

Third, 60% of SaaS sites already publish llms.txt, yet we found no engine documenting that it reads the file for answers. Google also says [no special schema.org markup is needed for AI features](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features). Keep both as cheap hygiene, not as levers.

sections.heading: Which tactics move SaaS AI visibility?
sections.body:
Fix third-party coverage first, then your own factual pages. Our ranking, from most to least leverage:

1. **Get into the roundups.** "Best [category] software" and "[competitor] alternatives" articles are built as candidate lists, so fan-out searches return them. List the roundups that appear for your 15 prompts and pitch each editor with facts: price, integrations, who you suit.
2. **Build a specific review profile.** G2 reports that [45% of buyers call a review-site citation the most confidence-inspiring signal](https://learn.g2.com/g2-2026-ai-search-insight-report) in an AI answer. Ask customers to name the problem solved and the tools they compared; detail gives engines something to quote.
3. **Publish facts, not slogans.** In the GEO paper, adding statistics, quotations and cited sources raised visibility by [30-40% on its position-adjusted word-count metric](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735), while keyword stuffing underperformed. Put pricing, limits and integration lists in plain tables.
4. **Say who you are not for.** "Best for 10 to 200 seats, no SSO on the starter plan" earns you the constrained queries. Vague positioning gets summarized into nothing.
5. **Mark up the basics.** Organization and SoftwareApplication schema state who you are. Google's software app rich result [requires a name, a price and a rating or review](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/software-app), but that is a search feature, not an AI lever.

We would not spend this quarter on schema tweaks or llms.txt. The [full playbook](/blog/how-to-get-your-business-recommended-by-ai) covers the general steps.

![Four colleagues working with laptops and documents at a shared desk, seen from above.](https://images.pexels.com/photos/7653569/pexels-photo-7653569.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1200)

sections.heading: How should a SaaS team measure it?
sections.body:
Run a fixed set of real buyer prompts on every engine, repeat them, and report how often you are named, with the denominator. One answer is a sample, not a rate: in SparkToro's 2,961 runs by 600 volunteers, [the chance of getting the same brand list twice in 100 runs was under 1 in 100](https://sparktoro.com/blog/new-research-ais-are-highly-inconsistent-when-recommending-brands-or-products-marketers-should-take-care-when-tracking-ai-visibility/) for ChatGPT and Google's AI.

For each prompt, record:

- **Named or not**, and whether first.
- **The framing** the engine uses for you.
- **Which competitors** fill your slots. They point to the sources to target.
- **Which sources** the answer cites.

Write prompts the way your buyers do, with qualifiers, using your sales discovery notes. AEOeye's [free audit](/) asks three unbranded buyer questions to ChatGPT live and shows the answers and the competitors named. The $29 full report adds Claude, Gemini, Google AI and Perplexity and ten questions, one-time. For daily monitoring across hundreds of prompts, use a dedicated tracker; our [comparison of AI visibility tools](/blog/best-ai-visibility-tools) covers them.

sections.heading: What does a 30-day plan look like?
sections.body:
Spend week one measuring, two and three closing the biggest source gaps, and week four re-measuring with an owner named.

1. **Week 1, baseline.** Collect 15 to 20 high-intent prompts from sales calls. Run them on all five engines. Record the four fields above.
2. **Week 2, find the sources.** For every prompt a competitor wins, list the pages the engine cites. Rank them by how often they recur.
3. **Week 3, close the gap.** Pitch the top roundups, run a review push on G2 and Capterra, and publish or correct your comparison, pricing and integration pages. Fix stale prices the web is repeating.
4. **Week 4, re-measure.** Re-run the same prompts the same way and diff against week one. Give one person the metric.

Changes can take weeks to show, because the pages that carry them must be published, indexed and retrieved. Judge the plan on the second run, not the first.

keyTakeaways: The "best tool for X" answer is the SaaS shortlist, and answers name only a few vendors.
In our study, 1 of 193 SaaS sites blocked an AI retrieval bot; being absent from third-party sources is the real gap.
Roundups and review profiles outrank your own blog for leverage; your own pages should carry hard facts.
Measure with fixed prompts and repeated runs, and report the rate with its denominator.
Run the 30-day plan once, then re-measure with a named owner.

faqs.q: What is AI visibility for SaaS?
faqs.a: It is how often AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI name your product when a buyer asks a buying question like "best tool for X", and how they describe you. For SaaS it matters because that answer now forms the buyer's shortlist before they visit your site or speak to sales.

faqs.q: How is it different from SEO for a SaaS company?
faqs.a: SEO competes for a ranked link the buyer may click. AI visibility is whether you are named in a written answer at all, and that answer leans on earned media such as roundups and reviews. The two overlap, since Google says existing SEO fundamentals still apply to its AI features, but backlinks to your own pages are only part of the picture.

faqs.q: Why does my product appear for the broad category but not specific queries?
faqs.a: Qualified prompts, such as "best help desk for Shopify stores", are answered from narrower sets of sources, and you may be absent from them. The fix is coverage: roundups, reviews and your own pages that state the segment, integration or compliance fit in plain words, so a retrieval step can match you.

faqs.q: Should we block GPTBot to protect our content?
faqs.a: Blocking GPTBot only opts out of OpenAI model training; OpenAI says each bot's setting is independent, and OAI-SearchBot controls whether you appear in ChatGPT search. Only 4 of 193 SaaS sites in our study blocked GPTBot. If buyers finding you in ChatGPT matters, keep OAI-SearchBot allowed.

faqs.q: How do I see what AI assistants say about my SaaS today?
faqs.a: Ask your real buyer questions on each engine, several times, and record who is named and how. AEOeye's free audit does this for three unbranded questions on ChatGPT, showing the full answers and the competitors named. The $29 report adds four more engines and ten questions.
